In most common law jurisdictions (including the UK, US, Canada, and Australia), a landowner has the legal right to cut back any branches or roots from a neighbor's tree that overhang onto their property, provided the cut is made up to the property line and does not extend into the neighbor's land. This right exists to protect one's own property from damage or obstruction, such as the shading of your neighbor's vegetable bed.

However, while your neighbor was legally within his rights to perform the cut, his manner of doing so was likely poor etiquette. He was not required to ask for your permission, but leaving the cut branches on your side of the boundary is generally considered a breach of duty. In many places, the branches (and the fruit) technically remain your property once cut, and the neighbor is often obligated to return them or at least offer them to you. By leaving them on your side without a word, he may have technically committed a minor trespass or conversion, even if his initial act of pruning was lawful.

Your anger is understandable, particularly given the sentimental value of the tree your late husband planted. While the law supports his right to trim the encroachment, the lack of communication and the failure to return the cuttings show a lack of neighborly consideration. A better approach would have been to knock on your door, explain the shading issue, and perhaps offer to do the work himself or ask for your permission to proceed, even though he didn't legally have to.
